passage: The auto slowed at the big junction near the vegetable market, and Pooja's hand went to the seat rail, the way it had every day since the scooter crash last winter. This time she counted the flower stalls instead: one, two, three heaps of marigolds. Her routine held her up: chai with Jagdish Mama at seven, college by nine, Thursday sessions with a trained therapist at the clinic above the chemist. At a cousin's wedding the week before, an aunt had leaned in. "Tell us everything, what exactly happened?" Pooja smiled. "I'm safe now. That's the part I want to talk about." Jagdish Mama had quietly steered the aunt toward the sweets. Today the junction slid past. Pooja noticed she had been thinking about her exam, not the crash. She still remembered it. It just didn't grab her by the throat anymore.

qa.q: When does Pooja see the trained therapist?
qa.a: She has Thursday sessions with a trained therapist at the clinic above the chemist.

qa.q: Why did Pooja answer the aunt with "I'm safe now" instead of telling the whole story?
qa.a: She felt uneasy retelling the crash on demand, and wanted to keep control over what she shared, so she chose the part she was comfortable with.

qa.q: What choice did Pooja make at the junction this time, and why did it help?
qa.a: She counted the flower stalls instead of bracing in fear, which kept her mind in the present until the junction passed.

qa.q: How might Jagdish Mama see Pooja's healing when he steers the aunt away?
qa.a: He seems to understand that she is recovering at her own pace, and wants to protect her right to share only what feels right.

grounding: It shows a young adult recovering from a crash through safety, steady routines, a trained therapist and choosing what to share, with the memory losing its hold.

passage:
Monsoon rain drummed on the hostel window. Gargi, Shreya's roommate, lowered her voice.
"Is the rain bad for you?"
"You don't have to whisper, Gargi. I can talk about the flood. Some of it."
"Sorry. My aunt knows a yoga teacher who does 'trauma healing'. Want the number?"
"Thanks, but I've booked the campus counselling centre. I checked, the counsellor there is trained for this."
"And the five a.m. alarm every day? Is that part of it?"
"Walk, bath, lecture notes. Same order, every day. When it rains, the order holds me."
"Do you want to tell me what happened that night?"
"Not tonight. Maybe never all of it. Is that okay?"
"Of course it is. Chai?"
"Yes. And Gargi? I don't think I'll ever forget the water in our stairwell. I just want to hear rain and not jump up."
The drizzle thickened. Shreya stayed on her bed, both hands around her cup.

qa.q: What does Shreya do every day after the five a.m. alarm?
qa.a: Walk, bath, lecture notes, in the same order, every day.

qa.q: How does Shreya feel when Gargi asks about that night, and what shows it?
qa.a: Shreya still feels it is too painful to retell and seems unsure that is allowed; she says "Not tonight. Maybe never all of it" and checks whether that is okay.

qa.q: Which choice did Shreya make about getting help, and why was it sound?
qa.a: She booked the campus counselling centre after checking the counsellor was trained, instead of taking an untrained healer's number.

qa.q: What is it like for Gargi to hear "Not tonight"?
qa.a: Gargi may feel unsure how to help, but by simply offering chai she learns that support can mean respecting Shreya's limits.

grounding: It shows a young adult after a flood keeping a steady routine, choosing a trained counsellor, sharing only what feels right and hoping for the past to loosen its hold.

passage: A year after the car accident, I can drive past that junction again. I'm Jasleen, and I want to say how I got here, because it wasn't by forcing myself. First I made my room feel safe: a lamp by the bed, the door I could lock. I kept small routines, the same morning walk, chai at seven, calling Nani on Sundays. I didn't tell everyone the story; I told two friends what I was ready to say, and nothing more. Then I found a therapist, Manoj, who was trained in trauma. We went slowly. I still remember the crash. Some nights it still comes back. But it doesn't grab me by the throat any more. It's a memory now, not a place I live.

qa.q: What did Jasleen keep beside the bed?
qa.a: A lamp.

qa.q: How does Jasleen feel about the memory of the crash now?
qa.a: Jasleen feels calmer and freer, still remembering it but no longer gripped by fear.

qa.q: Which steps helped Jasleen recover gently?
qa.a: Making the room feel safe, keeping routines, sharing only what felt right with two friends and working slowly with a trained therapist.

qa.q: How might Manoj see Jasleen's progress?
qa.a: Manoj likely sees that the memory is still there but has lost its grip, which is what recovery looks like.

grounding: Shows a young adult prioritising safety, keeping routines, sharing only what feels right and choosing a trained therapist, so the past loses its grip.

passage:
Warden's note, men's hostel, Block B.
Shankar, twenty, moved in here three months ago after the fire at his old paying-guest house. At first he slept with the lights on and jumped at every door bang. I've watched how he has handled things. He asked for a ground-floor room near the exit, which we gave him. He keeps a strict routine: gym at six, classes, dinner at eight, lights off at eleven. When the boys asked what happened, he said, "A fire. I'll talk more someday," and left it there. He sees a trauma therapist at the city hospital every Thursday.
This week there was a fire drill. He walked out calmly with everyone else. Afterwards he told me, "I still remember everything. It just doesn't take over." — Sarita

qa.q: What day does Shankar see his therapist?
qa.a: He sees his trauma therapist every Thursday.

qa.q: How did Shankar seem to feel during the fire drill?
qa.a: He seemed calm and steady, walking out with everyone else instead of panicking.

qa.q: What choices helped Shankar recover?
qa.a: Asking for a room near the exit, keeping a strict routine, sharing only what he wanted and seeing a trained trauma therapist.

qa.q: How might the other boys see Shankar after the drill?
qa.a: They may see him as steady and strong, respecting that he shares his story in his own time.

grounding: Shows a young adult prioritising safety, routine, sharing only what feels right and seeing a trained therapist, so the past no longer takes over.

passage:
Saturday
Today we drove past the place where the bus crashed last year. I told Bhupen before we left, "I might go quiet." He just nodded.
My hands got cold. I looked at the broken railing, now fixed, and I felt sad. But I didn't freeze. I didn't need to get out of the car.
A year ago I couldn't even hear a horn without shaking. What changed? My therapist says it's the small things: sleeping in the same room with the window I trust, dinner at the same time with Ma, telling people only what I'm ready to. And every Tuesday, her room with the green chair, where I can say anything.
I'll never forget the crash. But today it felt like it was behind me.
Pradeep

qa.q: What had been fixed at the crash site?
qa.a: The broken railing had been fixed.

qa.q: How did Pradeep feel passing the crash site?
qa.a: Pradeep felt sad and a bit shaky, with cold hands, but not frozen or panicked.

qa.q: What has helped Pradeep recover?
qa.a: Regular sessions with a trained therapist, a safe room, steady routines like dinner with Ma, and sharing only what feels right.

qa.q: How might Bhupen have felt when Pradeep warned about going quiet?
qa.a: Bhupen probably felt trusted and calm, simply nodding and giving Pradeep space.

grounding: Shows a young adult who keeps safety and routine, shares selectively and works with a trained therapist, finding the memory remains but loses its grip.

passage:
Harish: How was the session today?
Jaya: Good, actually. Fourth one. I think I trust her now.
Harish: That's big. Do you want to tell me what you talked about?
Jaya: Not the details. Those stay with her for now. Is that okay?
Harish: Of course. You share what feels right.
Jaya: She said to keep my days steady. So: college, gym at 6, dinner with you guys, lights off by 11.
Jaya: I also changed my route home. The busy road feels safer.
Harish: Smart. Want me to walk with you on Thursdays?
Jaya: Yes please, bhaiya.
Jaya: Weird thing. I thought getting better meant forgetting the accident. It doesn't. I still remember. It just doesn't grab me by the throat every hour anymore.
Harish: That sounds like it's losing its grip.
Jaya: Yeah. Slowly.

qa.q: How many therapy sessions has Jaya had?
qa.a: Four; today was the fourth one.

qa.q: How does Jaya feel about the therapist now?
qa.a: Jaya feels a growing trust and some relief, saying the sessions are going well.

qa.q: What parts of Jaya's approach support her recovery?
qa.a: Putting safety first with a safer route, keeping a steady routine, sharing only what feels right and working with a trained therapist.

qa.q: How might Harish feel when Jaya says the details stay with the therapist?
qa.a: He might feel a flicker of wanting to know, but mostly respect and relief that Jaya is getting proper support.

grounding: Jaya prioritises safety and routine, shares only what feels right and works with a trained therapist, finding that recovery is the past losing its grip, not forgetting.
